Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. They will match the nouns they modify in number, gender and case.

Adjectives frequently use a 2-1-2 paradigm:

masculine = 2nd declension forms,
feminine = 1st declension forms, and
neuter = 2nd declension forms.

When an adjective's root ends in an epsilon, iota, or rho, the "a" 1st declension form will be used.

Introduction

Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. They will match the nouns they modify in number, gender and case.

Adjectives frequently use a 2-1-2 paradigm:

masculine = 2nd declension forms,
feminine = 1st declension forms, and
neuter = 2nd declension forms.

When an adjective's root ends in an epsilon, iota, or rho, the "a" 1st declension form will be used.

εἰμί is a stative verb (it indicates a state of being) and so has no voice (active, middle, passive).

In English "is" takes a predicate nominative rather than the normal accusative. It is correct to say "This is he" and incorrect to say "This is him." Similarly in Greek a noun or pronoun in the nominative follows the verb εἰμί.

Types of Pronouns

There are various types of Pronouns:

Personal pronouns: stand in for a person—"Bill did it. He was there."
Demonstrative pronouns: point to a person or object which is near (this/these) or far (that/those).
Relative pronouns: relate a subordinate clause to a noun—"It is a great person who attempts to master Greek."
Reciprocal pronouns: state an interchange between two things/persons—They loved one another.
Reflexive pronouns: direct the action of the verb back to the subject—"She hid herself behind the door."
Interrogative pronouns: ask a question—Who broke the chair?

Subjective—which are used when a pronoun is the subject of a sentence (He turned left).
Possessive—which are used to indicate ownership (He gave his best).
Objective—which are used when a pronoun is the object of a sentence (He left him).

The third person pronoun αὐτός differs from the first and second person pronouns in that it is marked for gender. With first and second person pronouns, there is no need to specify gender because it is understood as the one speaking or one being spoken to.

αὐτός also has some other special features which we will examine here.

topics.text:
Demonstratives

Demonstratives are pointers. They point to things near ("this/these") or things far ("that/those"). "These" and "those" are the plural forms.

Demonstratives may function like adjectives when they modify a word, or like pronouns when they stand alone.

Adjective: "He bought this computer."
Pronoun: "This is the computer."

Relatives

Relative pronouns are words like: who, whom, which, that and whose.

They are often embedded in clauses that modify a noun. "Who" is usually used for humans and "which" for non-humans. "Whose" is used for both.

The student who loves Greek will succeed.
The keys which were lost in the river are gone forever.

Greek has two demonstratives:

ἐκεῖνος
that (plural = those)
οὗτος/αὕτη/τοῦτο
this (plural = these)

These can function either like a pronoun (when they stand alone) or like an adjective (thus agreeing with their antecedent in gender, number and case).

320.text:
Introduction

A relative pronoun often introduces a subordinate clause relating one word or idea to this clause. They agree with their antecedent in gender and number. Their case is determined by their role in the sentence or clause. Relatives are usually translated as "who" or "whom" for humans and "which" for neuter. "That" and "whose" can be used for either humans or non-humans. (Mounce, p. 109)

Sometimes the relative pronoun will have the case of its antecedent rather than the case that it should have within its own clause.
Sometimes the antecedent is understood in the context and not explicitly stated.

Augments

The augment is added in 4 ways:

before consonants it is "ε"
before vowels the augment contracts with the vowel according to the following rules:
α + ε = η ε + ε = η ο + ε = ω
ει + ε = ῃ αι + ε = ῃ οι + ε = ῳ
αυ + ε = ηυ ευ + ε = ηυ
Contraction Examples
Compound verbs with prepositions ending in a consonant: insert the augment between the prepositional prefix and the verb stem.
ἐκβάλλω becomes ἐξεβάλλον
Compound verbs with prepositions ending in a vowel: the final vowel of the preposition is dropped and the ε augment inserted in its place.
ἀποκτείνω becomes ἀπέκτεινον

states.text:
Introduction

The Greek imperfect tense is used when continuous or repeated action in the past is being referred to.

In English it will usually be translated with the helping verb was/were + the participle form of the verb (e.g. was singing).

Verbs that are deponent in the present tense are also deponent in the imperfect.
